description: Six minds, one shared curiosity, and an endless universe of possibilities. United by our love for space, science, and technology, we believe the best ideas begin with curiosity and grow through collaboration. We're here to think beyond boundaries, turn bold ideas into reality, and make our little contribution to something much bigger. Here's to exploring the unknown, together.
summary:
KURO – Lunar South Pole Navigator

At the Moon’s South Pole the Sun skims the horizon and Earth hangs low in the sky, so a few metres of terrain decide whether a lander has power and can call home. IM-2 Athena, planned for about ten days on the surface, lasted less than thirteen hours.

KURO is a browser-based tool that makes this easy to see. Pick a landing date and stay length, and KURO scores 78 candidate sites in nine South Pole regions out of 100 in under a second. It weighs flat ground, safety, sunlight, Earth contact, and power plus radio together. Every reason is explained in plain words, and the Sun and Earth are plotted against each site’s real skyline. You can explore any site in 3D, from the whole Moon down to a drivable rover, and compare the best four side by side on one shared clock.

Everything is computed from NASA data. Sun and Earth positions come from JPL DE421 and are checked against JPL Horizons to within 0.02°. Terrain and skylines come from LOLA elevation models, traced out to 300 km, and imagery comes from LRO via Moon Trek. 148 automated tests pass.

KURO helps mission planners, educators and the public compare landing sites and dates by the sunlight and Earth contact they get.
details:
KURO is a browser app that helps anyone compare landing sites near the Moon’s South Pole. You choose a landing date, time and stay length (7 to 120 days). For every candidate site, KURO samples the stay about every 15 minutes and checks whether the Sun and Earth stand above that site’s real skyline.

Sun and Earth positions come from NASA JPL’s DE421 ephemeris and are checked against JPL Horizons to within 0.02°.

Skylines are traced in 360 directions out to 300 km over NASA LOLA elevation data.

Scoring: each of the 78 candidate sites in nine regions gets a score out of 100. It weighs flat ground (25%), safety (25%), sunlight (20%), Earth contact (15%), and power plus radio together (15%).

You can then open any site’s reasons in plain words, explore it in 3D from orbit down to a drivable rover, and compare the best four sites side by side on a shared clock.

Benefits

Screening that used to take hours across several NASA tools now takes seconds, on one page.

Every result is explained, not just ranked.

It runs in any browser with no installation, account or API keys.

Every number is traceable to NASA data and independently validated, with 148 automated tests.

Intended impact

Mission planners: a fast first-pass screen of sites and dates.

Educators: a ready-made lesson on why the lunar South Pole is special.

The public: an honest, engaging way to understand real missions such as IM-2 Athena, whose planned ten-day mission lasted less than thirteen hours.

Tools and technology

Languages: TypeScript, Python, HTML and CSS.

Libraries and frameworks: React 19, Three.js for 3D, Zustand, GSAP, Vite and Vitest.

NASA data: JPL DE421, JPL Horizons, LOLA elevation models (PGDA product 90 and LDEM_16), the LRO WAC mosaic via Moon Trek, LROC QuickMap, and the Artemis III candidate regions.

Hardware: standard laptops. The site runs on ordinary computers, with a lite mode for low-end devices.

AI assistance:

Claude and Codex for code.

ChatGPT and Perplexity for research.

ChatGPT and Gemini for concept images.

Google Flow for the video.

Claude and Miro AI for documentation and flowchart layouts.

Creativity

KURO turns dry geometry into a story. The home page retells Athena’s “thirteen hours” through KURO, a friendly rover guide. You don’t just read a score: you can drive a rover across real NASA terrain at the site and watch the Sun and Earth move across its skyline. Scientific data, plain language and play sit together in one experience.

Factors we considered

Scientific accuracy: validation against JPL Horizons and published illumination studies.

Honesty: no invented data, clear limitations, and simulated elements labelled as such.

Accessibility: plain language and guided tours.

Performance: fast ranking, a lightweight 3D model, and drawing only when the view changes.

Ease of deployment: a static site that needs no server.
